svg.text: Burns: the first twenty minutes, then the first twenty-four hours
Most harm in Ghanaian burns is done twice — once by the fire, and once by what is applied to it afterwards.
First aid that works
Stop the burning. Remove clothing and
jewellery before swelling starts.
Cool running water for twenty minutes.
Cool the burn, but keep the patient warm.
Cover with a clean cloth or cling film.
Water still helps up to about three hours later.
What is commonly applied, and why not
Palm oil, shea butter, toothpaste, egg,
powdered herbs, engine oil, ice.
They hold the heat in, introduce infection,
and hide the depth of the burn.
Ice causes a second, cold injury on top.
Ask what was applied. Do not scold — you need to know.
Estimating the area burnt
Adults, rule of nines: head 9, each arm 9,
each leg 18, front 18, back 18, perineum 1.
The patient's own palm with fingers is
about 1 per cent — useful for scattered burns.
A child is not a small adult
A young child's head is proportionally much
larger and the legs much shorter, so the
adult rule of nines overestimates the legs
and underestimates the head.
Judging whether the resuscitation is working
The formula gives a starting rate, not an answer. The measurement that tells you whether it is enough is the urine
output, hour by hour — around 0.5 mL per kilogram per hour in an adult, and rather more in a child.
Titrate the fluid to the urine. Never run the calculated rate and stop looking.
